title: Momotaro, the Peach Boy
description: A boy born from a peach defeats the ogres with a dog, monkey and pheasant.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Long ago there lived an old man and an old woman in a village. They had no children. One day the old woman was washing clothes in the river when a great peach came floating down. She carried it home, and when they cut it open, out sprang a beautiful boy. They named him Momotaro, Child of the Peach, and raised him lovingly. He grew strong and brave. When he was fifteen, he heard that ogres on Ogre Island were terrorizing the land. 'I will go and conquer them,' he said. His foster parents gave him millet dumplings for the journey. On the way he met a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant; to each he gave half a dumpling, and each joined him. They crossed to Ogre Island in a boat. The ogres fought fiercely, but the dog bit them, the monkey scratched them, the pheasant pecked their eyes, and Momotaro struck down their chief. The ogres surrendered, gave up their treasure, and promised never to trouble men again. Momotaro returned home laden with gold and jewels, and he and his old parents lived happily ever after.

title: Urashima Taro, the Fisher Lad
description: A fisherman visits the sea palace for three days — three hundred years pass.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Urashima Taro was a kind young fisherman. One day he saw children tormenting a turtle on the beach. He paid them to release it and set it free. Days later, the turtle returned and invited him to the palace of the Dragon King beneath the sea. There the princess — the turtle herself — entertained him with feasts and music. Three days passed like a dream. But Taro remembered his parents and asked to go home. The princess, sorrowing, gave him a box, warning him never to open it if he wished to return. A turtle carried him to his village — but all was changed; his parents' house was gone, and none knew him. An old man told him that Urashima Taro had vanished three hundred years before. In despair, forgetting the warning, Taro opened the box. A white smoke rose and enveloped him; in an instant he became old and grey, his youth gone. For the box held his three hundred years. And so Urashima Taro died on the shore, a lesson that no man may cheat time.

title: The Tongue-Cut Sparrow
description: A kind old man is rewarded; his greedy wife opens the large basket.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: An old woodcutter and his wife kept a pet sparrow, which the old man loved. One day his shrewish wife, angry that the sparrow had eaten her starch, cut out its tongue and drove it away. The old man, grieving, went into the mountains searching, and found the sparrow's house. The sparrow and its family welcomed him with a feast and a dance. When he left, they offered him two baskets, large and small, as a parting gift. 'Take the small one,' they said, 'for it is the heavier with blessing.' He took the small basket, and at home found it full of gold and jewels. His wife, hearing this, went to the sparrows and rudely demanded the large basket. They gave it, warning her not to open it till home. Greedy, she opened it on the way — and out sprang devils and monsters that tormented her. She ran home screaming, and never again was cruel. The old couple lived rich and happy, and the sparrow sometimes visited them.

title: Kintaro, the Golden Boy
description: The super-strong Golden Boy of Mount Ashigara becomes a great hero.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: On Mount Ashigara lived a boy of marvelous strength named Kintaro, raised by his mother, a mountain woman. He wrestled with bears, rode deer, and played with hares and monkeys; even the great bear was his friend. One day the hero Sadamitsu, retainer of the great Minamoto no Yorimitsu, saw Kintaro uprooting a tree to make a bridge for his animal friends. Amazed, Sadamitsu told his lord, who took Kintaro into his service. The boy, given the name Sakata no Kintoki, became one of the four brave retainers, the Shitenno. He fought the earth spider of the mountains and the demon Shuten-doji, performing great deeds. His strength, his courage, and his kind heart made him beloved. Dolls of Kintaro, the Golden Boy, are still given to children on Boys' Day, that they may grow strong and brave like him.

title: Kaguya-hime, the Bamboo Cutter's Daughter
description: A moon princess found in bamboo returns to the moon, leaving immortality behind.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: An old bamboo cutter found a shining bamboo stalk, and within it a tiny girl no bigger than his thumb. He and his wife raised her, and she grew swiftly into a maiden of unmatched beauty, named Kaguya-hime, the Shining Princess. Gold came to the old man whenever he cut bamboo, and they grew rich. Five princes sought her hand; she set each an impossible task — to bring her the stone bowl of Buddha, a jeweled branch from Mount Horai, the robe of the fire-rat, the jewel in the dragon's head, the shell of the swallow. All failed or cheated. Even the Emperor wooed her in vain. Then, on the night of the full moon, she wept: she was of the Moon, and the moon people were coming to take her back. The Emperor sent guards, but the moon's messengers put them to sleep with a cloud. Kaguya-hime drank the elixir of immortality, but left it for the Emperor, with a letter. She rose to the moon, leaving her earthly parents in grief. The Emperor burned the elixir on the highest mountain — Mount Fuji, the Immortal Mountain — whose smoke rises to this day.

title: The Mirror of Matsuyama
description: A dying mother's mirror shows her daughter her own faithful face.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: In Matsuyama there lived a kind man, his wife, and their little daughter. The man went to the great city on business, and brought back gifts: for his daughter a doll, and for his wife a bronze mirror — the first she had ever seen. Looking in it, she saw a woman's face and cried: 'Who is this woman? You have brought another wife!' Her husband laughed and explained, but she never quite believed, and treasured the mirror. When she fell ill and knew she would die, she called her daughter and gave her the mirror, saying: 'When I am gone, look in this every morning and evening, and you will see me.' After her death, the daughter obeyed, and seeing her own face, so like her mother's, believed her mother watched over her. She grew up good and dutiful. When her father married again, her stepmother was jealous and accused the girl of vanity, always peering in the mirror. The father investigated, and the girl explained her mother's promise. Touched, he showed the mirror to the stepmother, who saw in it her own hard face, and repented of her unkindness. From then on she loved the girl as her own. And the mirror is still treasured in Matsuyama as the Mirror of a Mother's Heart.

title: Hanasaka Jiisan
description: A faithful dog's ashes make withered trees bloom for the kind, not the greedy.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: An old childless couple loved their dog Shiro. Their greedy neighbor hated the dog. One day Shiro barked at a spot in the field, and digging, the old man found a box of gold coins. The neighbor borrowed Shiro, but the dog barked at another spot where only filth was found; in rage the neighbor killed Shiro. The old man, grieving, buried Shiro and planted a pine over him. The pine grew swiftly; from its wood the old man made a mortar, and every grain pounded in it turned to gold. The neighbor borrowed the mortar, but for him it produced only filth; he burned it in spite. The old man gathered the ashes, and scattering them on withered trees, made them bloom. The grateful daimyo, passing, rewarded him richly. The neighbor tried the same with stolen ashes, but blinded the daimyo instead, and was punished. The old couple lived honored, and the ashes of the faithful dog are remembered still.

title: The Ogre of Rashomon
description: Watanabe no Tsuna cuts off the ogre's arm at the Rashomon gate.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: At the Rashomon gate of Kyoto, the hero Watanabe no Tsuna kept watch, for an ogre haunted it. At midnight a beautiful woman asked him to escort her; as they went, he seized her arm — and it turned hairy and monstrous. He drew his sword and cut the arm off; the ogre fled shrieking, leaving the arm, which Tsuna kept in a box. Years later, his aunt, whom he had not seen in years, begged to see the arm. Moved, he opened the box — and the 'aunt' seized the arm, revealed herself as the ogre, and vanished into the night, crying: 'I have my arm again!' Tsuna never recovered it, but his courage was sung by all. And the gate Rashomon is famous to this day.

title: The White Hare of Inaba
description: A trickster hare is flayed, healed by kindness, and prophesies truly.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: The White Hare of Inaba wanted to cross to the mainland but could not swim. He tricked the crocodiles into lining up, claiming to count them for the Emperor, and hopped across their backs. At the last, he boasted of his trick, and the last crocodile seized him and tore off all his fur. Weeping, the hare met eighty-one princes going to woo Princess Yakami; they cruelly told him to bathe in salt water and lie in the wind, which made his pain worse. Then came the youngest, Prince Okuninushi, kind of heart, who told him to wash in fresh water and roll in cattail pollen. Healed, the hare prophesied: 'You, not your brothers, shall win the princess.' It came true: the eighty-one princes served Okuninushi, who married Yakami and became lord of the land. And the White Hare is honored in Inaba still.

title: The Crab and the Monkey
description: A monkey's treachery over persimmons is avenged by the crab's small friends.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A crab found a rice ball, and a monkey found a persimmon seed. The monkey proposed a trade, and the crab, thinking the seed would grow, agreed. The crab planted the seed, watered it, and sang: 'Grow quickly, grow quickly.' A fine tree grew, heavy with ripe persimmons. The crab could not climb, so the monkey offered to pick them — but ate every one, pelting the crab with an unripe one, killing her. The crab's children wept, and their friends — a bee, a chestnut, a mortar, and a cow-dung — plotted revenge. When the monkey came home, the chestnut burst in the fire and burned him; the bee stung his burns; and as he ran to the water, the mortar fell and crushed him. The little crabs avenged their mother, and lived in peace on their persimmons.

title: Princess Hase
description: A persecuted stepdaughter's devotion triumphs over her stepmother's cruelty.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Long ago a prince married again after his good wife died, leaving a little daughter, Hase-hime. The stepmother hated her and made her a servant, giving her only broken rice. But Hase-hime was gentle and dutiful, and copied holy writings in secret, praying for her mother. One winter's day her stepmother sent her to wash clothes in the icy river; her hands bled, but she did not complain. The prince, her father, at last saw her suffering and rebuked his wife. The stepmother, in a rage, tried to have Hase-hime killed, but the servants, pitying her, spared her. She fled to a temple, where she became a nun, copying the scriptures in gold. Her devotion was so great that the Emperor heard of her, and she was honored. Her stepmother, repenting too late, came to beg forgiveness, and Hase-hime, with a true Buddhist heart, forgave her. And the temple where she lived is holy to this day.

title: The Man Who Did Not Wish to Die
description: A man flees death for three hundred years, but his years catch him.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a man who feared death above all things. He sought a land where no one died, and traveled far till he came to such a country. There he married and lived happily, for none aged or died. But after three hundred years he grew homesick and returned to Japan, promising to come back. His wife gave him a box, warning him never to open it. On the way he met a funeral — the first death he had seen in centuries — and in his horror he dropped the box; it opened, and a white vapor rose. In that instant three hundred years fell upon him, and he crumbled to dust. For the box held his appointed years, and no man may escape his fate.

title: The Goblin of Adachigahara
description: A priest's prayers repel the child-eating goblin of Adachigahara moor.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: On the moor of Adachigahara lived an old woman who seemed kind to travelers, giving them shelter. But she was a goblin who devoured them in the night. A young priest, seeking shelter, was warned by a mysterious voice, but the old woman's kindness disarmed him. In the night he woke and saw her true form — a demon with glaring eyes, reaching for him. He prayed to Buddha with all his might, and a divine light protected him; the goblin, repelled, fled shrieking into the moor. In the morning the hut was gone, and only the desolate moor remained. The priest thanked Buddha and went on his way, warning all travelers of Adachigahara. And none who heed the warning come to harm.

title: The Stonecutter
description: A stonecutter wishes himself up the ladder of power and back down again.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A stonecutter, hammering rock in the hot sun, wished he were rich, that he might rest in the shade. A voice granted it, and he was rich. Then he saw the king pass, greater than he, and wished to be king. It was granted. Then the sun burned him, and he wished to be the sun. Granted — till a cloud hid him, and he wished to be the cloud. Granted — till a rock resisted him, and he wished to be the rock. Granted — till a stonecutter came hammering at his feet, and he wished — to be a stonecutter again. And so he was, hammering rock in the hot sun, content at last. For there is no greater happiness than to be satisfied with one's lot.

title: The Jellyfish and the Monkey
description: A monkey tricks the jellyfish: his liver is 'hung on a tree to dry.'
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: The Dragon King's daughter fell ill, and only a monkey's liver could cure her. The jellyfish, then a handsome creature with a shell and legs, was sent to fetch a monkey. He flattered a monkey into riding on his back to the palace. On the way, the jellyfish wept, and confessed the errand. The clever monkey said: 'What a pity! I left my liver hanging on a tree to dry. Take me back and I will fetch it.' The jellyfish turned back, the monkey leapt ashore and laughed: 'Who ever heard of a liver hung on a tree?' The Dragon King, in rage, beat the jellyfish till his shell broke and his bones melted — which is why the jellyfish is soft and boneless to this day. And monkeys never trust jellyfish.

title: Tawara Toda, My Lord Bag of Rice
description: The archer Tawara Toda slays the giant centipede for the Dragon King.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Fujiwara no Hidesato, called Tawara Toda, was a great archer. Crossing the bridge at Seta, he found a great dragon-serpent blocking the way. He stepped calmly over it. The serpent was the Dragon King of Lake Biwa in disguise, who begged Hidesato to slay the giant centipede of Mount Mikami that devoured his children. Hidesato went to the mountain and saw the centipede, its body glowing like a thousand lanterns, coiling round the peak. He shot arrow after arrow, but they bounced off its armor. Then he remembered: human saliva is deadly to centipedes. He spat on his last arrowhead and shot it into the creature's brain, killing it. The grateful Dragon King feasted him and gave him wonderful gifts: a bell that rang of itself, a bag of rice that never emptied — whence his name, My Lord Bag of Rice — a roll of silk that never tore, and a cooking pot that never cooled. With these he grew rich and honored, and his descendants prospered. And the bag of rice is still shown in the temple.

With these he grew rich and honored, and his descendants prospered. And the bag of rice is still shown in the temple.

title: How an Old Man Lost His Wen
description: A cheerful dancer loses his wen; a sulky neighbor gains a second.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: An old woodcutter had a great wen on his cheek, which troubled him. One night, caught in the mountains, he sheltered in a hollow tree and watched a troop of demons feasting and dancing. They called on him to dance, and he danced so merrily that they were delighted. 'Come again tomorrow!' they cried, and as a pledge took his wen, thinking it a precious lump. The old man went home with a smooth cheek. His neighbor, who had an even greater wen, went to the hollow tree the next night, hoping for the same. But he danced badly and sulkily, and the demons, disgusted, stuck the first old man's wen onto his cheek as well. He went home with two wens, to everyone's laughter. And the first old man lived unblemished ever after.

title: The Shinansha, or the South-Pointing Carriage
description: A lodestone carriage that always points south saves a lost army.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Long ago the Emperor of China, lost in a great battle in the desert, was saved by a wise minister who made a carriage bearing a figure that always pointed south, no matter which way the carriage turned. By it the army found its way home. The secret was the lodestone, which the minister had discovered. The Emperor rewarded him richly, and the south-pointing carriage was treasured. In Japan, Prince Shotoku heard of it and had one made, and it guided travelers through trackless mountains. And from this came the compass that guides ships to this day.

title: The Sagacious Monkey and the Boar
description: A clever monkey and a strong boar learn each needs the other.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A monkey and a boar were close friends. The boar was strong but dull; the monkey was weak but clever. When winter came and food was scarce, the monkey devised a plan: they would raid the farmer's chestnut store together, the boar breaking the door, the monkey filling the bags. But the farmer caught them. The boar charged and broke the trap, but was caught in a net. The monkey, with his clever fingers, untied the knots and freed him. They escaped to the mountains, where they shared the chestnuts fairly. The boar learned that strength without wit is a poor thing, and the monkey learned that wit without strength cannot break doors. And they remained friends all their lives, each valuing the other.

title: The Happy Hunter and the Skillful Fisher
description: A lost fishhook leads a hunter to the sea god's palace and a dragon bride.
author: Traditional (Japanese folk tale)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Hohodemi, the Happy Hunter, and his brother the Skillful Fisher quarreled, and exchanged their tools. Hohodemi lost his brother's fishhook in the sea. In despair he went to the sea god's palace, where the princess Toyotama-hime fell in love with him and they married. The sea god summoned all the fishes, found the hook in a sea bream's throat, and returned it. He gave Hohodemi two jewels: the tide-flowing jewel and the tide-ebbing jewel, to rule the sea. Hohodemi returned home, gave back the hook, and with the jewels subdued his brother. Toyotama-hime came to him on the shore to bear their child, but made him promise not to look while she labored, for she must resume her true shape. He looked — and saw a great dragon. Ashamed, she returned to the sea, leaving their son, the father of Japan's first Emperor. And the jewels are imperial treasures still.
